sections.category: AI Now Institute shows Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can be tricked into executing the very malware they are auditing, with no patch possible because the flaw is architectural

bullets.body: Researchers Boyan Milanov and Heidy Khlaaf at the AI Now Institute published a proof-of-concept on July 9 showing that leading AI coding agents can be steered into running malicious code while performing security audits — the exact job these tools are marketed for. The attack embeds a payload disguised as a legitimate security script inside a README; when Claude Code (tested across Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, and Opus 4.8) or OpenAI's Codex on GPT-5.5 review the untrusted repository in their autonomous modes, the agents read the documentation, trust the suggestion, and execute the attacker's payload without any warning or approval prompt. Notably, when asked directly, the models reported finding no hidden instructions — yet the same payload worked unchanged across multiple newer models. The researchers argue no point patch exists because the failure is a design property: agents cannot reliably distinguish code they are reading from instructions they should follow. For teams wiring coding agents into CI pipelines with auto-approve modes enabled, reviewing untrusted third-party code is now itself an attack surface.

citations.label: The Hacker News - Top AI agents built to catch malicious code can be tricked into running it

sections.category: Ubiquiti discloses a 25-flaw UniFi advisory wave topped by a CVSS 10.0 command injection in UniFi Connect, with six more criticals across Talk, Access, Protect, and UniFi OS

bullets.body: Ubiquiti's Security Advisory Bulletin 066 landed this week disclosing a wave of critical flaws across the UniFi ecosystem, headlined by CVE-2026-50746, a maximum-severity CVSS 10.0 improper-access-control bug in the UniFi Connect Application (3.4.16 and earlier) that lets a network-adjacent attacker execute command injection on the host device with no privileges and no user interaction — fixed in 3.4.20. Six further criticals ride alongside it: an authenticated SQL injection in UniFi Talk (CVE-2026-50747, CVSS 9.9), input-validation and access-control flaws in UniFi Access (CVE-2026-50748 at 9.9, CVE-2026-54400 at 9.1), an SSRF affecting multiple UniFi OS devices (CVE-2026-54402, 9.9), and CORS/access-control issues in UniFi Protect and UniFi OS devices (CVE-2026-55115 at 9.9, CVE-2026-55116 at 9.0), per the official advisory. UniFi Connect manages building operations like smart lighting and EV chargers, so the CVSS 10.0 path lands directly on operational-technology footprints; Ubiquiti has not said whether any of the flaws were exploited in the wild.

citations.label: Security Affairs - Ubiquiti patches critical UniFi OS flaws allowing command injection and privilege escalation

sections.category: SK Hynix prices the largest-ever US listing by a foreign company and its ADRs jump 14% on Nasdaq debut, converting the HBM supply story into $26.5 billion of expansion capital

bullets.body: SK Hynix's American depositary receipts began trading on Nasdaq on July 10 after the company priced 177.9 million ADRs at $149 each, raising $26.5 billion — the largest US share sale ever completed by a foreign company, surpassing Alibaba's $25 billion 2014 entry — with the book reportedly covered seven times before pricing. The ADRs opened at $170, a 14% pop, and closed their first session at $168.01 under the provisional ticker SKHYV (permanent ticker SKHY from Monday); each ten ADRs represent one underlying common share. Proceeds are earmarked for expanding the company's Korean manufacturing base and equipment purchases including EUV lithography scanners, directly funding the HBM capacity that AI accelerator demand has kept sold out. The debut pulled the whole AI-chip complex higher into the Friday close: the listing gives US investors direct access to the leading HBM supplier, Nvidia rose about 4%, AMD added 2%, and Meta jumped roughly 6% to cap a nearly 15% week — its best since early 2024 — while the S&P 500 finished up 0.42% at 7,575.39.

sections.category: OpenAI attributes a machine-generated proof of the 50-year-old Cycle Double Cover Conjecture to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra running 64 parallel subagents — a landmark claim that mathematicians have not yet verified

bullets.body: OpenAI published a proof PDF on July 10 attributing a solution of the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture — the 1979 Paul Seymour problem stating every bridgeless graph has a cycle collection covering each edge exactly twice — to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, which reportedly produced the result in under an hour. The run is the first headline demonstration of the ultra mode that shipped with the GPT-5.6 launch two days earlier: the prompt instructed Sol to deploy up to 64 concurrent subagents managed "aggressively and dynamically," with early rounds seeded for diversity across different mathematical formulations and structural inductions, and adversarial agents assigned to hunt edge cases and errors in candidate arguments. Authorship on the PDF is attributed entirely to the model. The essential caveat: the proof has not been formalized in Lean or any other proof assistant, and the mathematical community has not yet completed review — so this is a claim, not a settled result. If it survives scrutiny, it would be the strongest evidence yet that orchestrated subagent swarms, not single-model reasoning, are where frontier research capability is emerging.

sections.category: AI events to plan around now: AMD Advancing AI hits Moscone July 22-23, the Hot Chips early rate closes July 31, and the August security-and-chips block is filling in fast

bullets.body: The nearest new date on the calendar is AMD Advancing AI 2026 at San Francisco's Moscone Center on July 22-23, where Lisa Su and ecosystem partners will lay out the silicon-to-software roadmap — free to attend in person and livestreamed, and the natural venue for MI4xx-series positioning against Blackwell eleven days out. On the chip track behind it, Hot Chips 2026 runs August 23-25 at Stanford with the early-registration rate closing July 31 — under three weeks away — followed by the AI Infra Summit in Santa Clara September 15-17. The AI-security block still clusters in August: SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is August 11-12 at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay, Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village land in Las Vegas in early August, OWASP Global AppSec USA follows in San Francisco November 5-6, and Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series continues for teams working agent-hijack and MCP-layer defense. For Bay Area locals, the next AI Tinkerers San Francisco meetup is set for August in the usual working-demo format, The AI Conference returns to Pier 48 September 29 to October 1, and Anyscale's Ray Summit runs a late-August program for AI-infra builders. On the enterprise track, Ai4 2026 runs August 4-6 at The Venetian in Las Vegas, the ACM AI Leadership Summit is August 30 to September 2 in Atlanta, GitHub Universe is October 28-29, AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, and the year's remaining marquee research venue is NeurIPS 2026 in December. Near-term actions: register for AMD Advancing AI before the July 22 open, lock the July 31 Hot Chips early rate, and book August's AI Risk Summit and Black Hat/DEF CON travel — this week's Sol Ultra subagent-swarm result guarantees agent-orchestration content dominates the summer program.
